Your measured resolution is degraded compared to theory for these reasons:

**Transducer factors:**
- Finite aperture size limits diffraction-based resolution improvement
- Transducer bandwidth narrower than theoretical; higher frequency components attenuated
- Beam profile has sidelobes spreading energy outside the main lobe

**Medium/propagation:**
- Acoustic aberrations and scattering in your medium distort the wavefront
- Speed-of-sound heterogeneity causes phase distortion
- Attenuation is frequency-dependent; high frequencies are preferentially absorbed

**Instrumentation:**
- Electronic noise floor limits signal-to-noise ratio
- Time-gain compensation and filtering degrade resolution
- Beamforming artifacts if using phased arrays

**Detection:**
- Your receiver bandwidth may be limiting; theoretical assumes unlimited bandwidth
- Pulse length longer than predicted (ringdown from transducer damping)
- Post-processing filters smoothing the data

The 3-4× gap is typical. Most real systems run 2-10× worse than diffraction-limit theory because theory assumes ideal conditions (infinite bandwidth, perfect medium, point sources). Check your transducer specs against measured impulse response, measure actual -6dB bandwidth, and verify your medium's attenuation coefficient.
